newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope plans arduous 11-day Poland trip in May-June.
newsitem.headline: Pope plans arduous 11-day Poland trip in May-June.

text.p: Pope John Paul is to make a gruelling 11-day visit to his native Poland from May 31 to June 10, the Polish government information office said on Wednesday.

It will be the 76-year-old Pontiff's sixth and longest trip to his homeland since his election in 1978, embracing 12 towns and cities in the west and south, including a two-day break in his beloved mountain ski resort of Zakopane.
Doctors have advised the Pope to slow down and take more rest since the removal of his appendix last October.
He is to spend the first two days in the southwestern city of Wroclaw at the end of the 46th International Eucharistic Congress, and is also due to meet Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski there.

According to the schedule, which the government information office said had been confirmed by the Pope, other stops in the trip include Poland's holiest shrine of Czestochowa, Gniezno, Poznan, and Krakow -- where John Paul was archbishop until 1978 and where his parents are buried.
He is to meet Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz there on June 8.

The trip is likely to be an emotional experience for the Pope, whose momentous visits home before the 1989 fall of communism gave heart to those struggling for democracy, and who last visited, for one day only, in May 1995.

It also falls amid fierce campaigning for general elections late this year in which the secular-minded ruling ex-communists are facing a strong challenge from a new right-leaning alliance headed by the strongly pro-Catholic Solidarity trade union.

Religious issues are playing a key role in the campaign, especially as the government late last year pushed through a law easing Poland's previously strict anti-abortion law, despite anguished protests from the Pope and Solidarity.
Solidarity, which has promised to reverse the new abortion law, hopes the Pope's visit will inspire its supporters.

Relations between the Church and the ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) are also strained by the left-dominated parliament's reluctance to ratify a concordat treaty between Poland and the Vatican, which was signed in 1993 by a previous centre-right government.
The SLD says the treaty would give the Catholic Church too much influence over life in Poland.

Kwasniewski, an ex-communist who signed the abortion bill into law, but who says he wants understanding with the Church, is tentatively planned to visit the Pope early this year during a trip to Italy, the foreign ministry said last month.
The Pope's visit will be the longest of four foreign trips the Pope has planned for this year. The others are to Prague, Paris and Rio de Janeiro in Brazil.
